title: Deadlock Fundamentals
summary: Deadlock is a cycle of waiting where nobody can proceed. The four Coffman conditions and resource allocation graphs give you the vocabulary to spot one precisely, not just describe the symptom.

slides.markdown:
**Deadlock** is what happens when two or more threads or processes each hold a resource the other needs, and each is waiting for the other to let go — forever. Nobody is broken; nobody crashed; everybody is just permanently stuck waiting.

The classic real version: thread A locks mutex 1, then tries to lock mutex 2. Thread B locks mutex 2, then tries to lock mutex 1. Both wait forever. This topic gives you the precise vocabulary — the four Coffman conditions and resource allocation graphs — for recognizing and describing exactly why that happens, which is the foundation every prevention/avoidance/detection strategy builds on.

slides.sectionTitle: What deadlock is: a cycle of waiting
slides.markdown:
Precisely: deadlock is a state where a set of processes (or threads) are each waiting for a resource held by another process **in that same set**, forming a closed loop — process 1 waits for something process 2 holds, process 2 waits for something process 3 holds, ..., and the last process waits for something process 1 holds.

None of them can ever make progress, because progress for any one of them depends on another releasing a resource — and none of them will, because they're all equally stuck. Unlike a slow or overloaded system, deadlock doesn't resolve on its own no matter how long you wait; the only ways out are prevention/avoidance (structurally never letting the cycle form) or detection and recovery (finding the cycle and forcibly breaking it).

Deadlock can only happen if **all four** of these hold simultaneously (named after Edward Coffman, who formalized them in 1971):

1. **Mutual exclusion** — at least one resource can only be held by one process/thread at a time.
2. **Hold and wait** — a process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional resources currently held by others.
3. **No preemption** — a resource can only be released voluntarily by the process holding it; the OS can't forcibly take it back.
4. **Circular wait** — there's a cycle of processes, each waiting for a resource held by the next.

This is the single most-tested fact in this area, precisely because every prevention strategy is just "pick one condition and make it structurally impossible."

slides.sectionTitle: Code: two threads, two locks, opposite acquisition order

slides.markdown:
A **Resource Allocation Graph (RAG)** makes "who's stuck on whom" visual and precise. Processes and resources are both nodes. An arrow from a resource to a process (**assignment edge**) means that process currently holds that resource. An arrow from a process to a resource (**request edge**) means that process is waiting to acquire it.

The two-thread deadlock from the code slide draws as: Thread 1 → (assignment) mutexA, mutexB → (assignment) Thread 2, Thread 1 → (request) mutexB, Thread 2 → (request) mutexA. Trace the arrows and you'll find they form a closed loop — that loop *is* the deadlock, drawn out.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a resource allocation graph showing a cycle
slides.markdown:
![Resource allocation graph with a deadlock cycle](assets/resource-allocation-graph-cycle.svg)

The graph makes the cycle undeniable: following the arrows P1 → R2 → P2 → R1 → P1 traces a complete loop with no exit. This is the exact same situation as the two-mutex code example, just drawn as a graph instead of code — the visual form is what lets you scale this reasoning to systems with dozens of resources, where eyeballing the code directly becomes impractical.

assets.alt: Resource allocation graph with a deadlock cycle

slides.sectionTitle: Cycle in the graph — necessary but not always sufficient
slides.markdown:
For resources that only ever have **one instance** (a single mutex, a single file lock), a cycle in the resource allocation graph is both necessary *and* sufficient for deadlock — if you find a cycle, you have a deadlock, guaranteed.

For resources with **multiple instances** (a pool of 5 identical database connections, 3 identical printers), a cycle is necessary but **not sufficient**. It's possible to have a cycle in the graph while some process outside the cycle still holds a spare instance of a needed resource and will eventually release it, breaking the deadlock without any intervention. This is exactly why real detection algorithms (see Deadlock Detection & Recovery) don't just look for graph cycles — they track actual instance counts and reduce the graph step by step to check if every process can eventually finish.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: deadlock vs starvation vs livelock
slides.markdown:
| | Deadlock | Starvation | Livelock |
|---|---|---|---|
| Progress | Zero — everyone involved is permanently blocked | One or more processes make no progress, but others do | Everyone stays busy, but no one makes real progress |
| Cause | Circular resource wait | Unfair scheduling — one process always loses priority | Processes actively responding to each other, undoing progress |
| Example | Two threads, two locks, opposite order | A low-priority process always preempted by higher-priority ones | Two people repeatedly stepping aside for each other in a hallway, blocking each other every time |
| Detectable via a wait-for cycle? | Yes | No — no cycle, just unfairness | Not via a static graph — the state keeps changing |

**How to decide which you're seeing:** check CPU usage of the stuck processes — deadlocked processes are typically idle/blocked (0% CPU), while livelocked processes are actively burning CPU accomplishing nothing, and starved processes are runnable but simply never selected.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming any lock-ordering violation immediately deadlocks
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Thread 1 locks A then B, and thread 2 locks B then A somewhere else in the codebase — that's a deadlock waiting to happen, so it must deadlock in practice."

**Why it's wrong:** an opposite-order lock acquisition is a **deadlock hazard**, not a guaranteed deadlock. It only actually deadlocks if the timing lines up exactly wrong — thread 1 must acquire A and thread 2 must acquire B *before* either tries for the other lock. Most of the time, one thread finishes its whole critical section (acquiring and releasing both locks) before the other even starts, and nothing bad happens — which is exactly why these bugs are so dangerous: they can sit unnoticed in production for months.

**Correct model:** treat inconsistent lock ordering as a latent bug to fix regardless of whether it has deadlocked yet — code review and static analysis tools (like Go's race detector's lock-order checking, or `lockdep` in the Linux kernel) exist specifically because you can't rely on "it hasn't happened yet" as evidence of safety.

slides.sectionTitle: Why database transactions make deadlock nearly inevitable at scale
slides.markdown:
Deadlock isn't a rare, contrived scenario — it's a routine occurrence in any system with fine-grained locking and enough concurrency, most visibly in databases. Two transactions updating the same two rows in opposite order (transaction A updates row 1 then row 2, transaction B updates row 2 then row 1, both under row-level locks) is the exact two-mutex pattern from this topic, just with database rows instead of `pthread_mutex_t`s.

Because it's routine, production databases don't try to *prevent* it structurally (that would require globally ordering every row update across every transaction, which is impractical) — they run a detection algorithm and pick a victim to abort, covered fully in Deadlock Detection & Recovery. The staff-level takeaway: at sufficient concurrency and lock granularity, deadlock becomes a normal operating condition you design a response to, not an anomaly you can engineer away entirely.
